units.title: Currently there are no reasons to doubt the Riemann Hypothesis: The zeta function beyond the realm of computation
units.selection_reason: Farmer lays out the paper's program: evaluate published reasons to doubt RH by replacing raw extrapolation from computation with principles about zeros, values, randomness, and carrier-wave behavior.
units.context_limit: This is an introductory programmatic span; the detailed numbered Principles appear later.
units.interpretation:
Farmer's introduction proposes that many reasons to doubt RH come from using the wrong representation scale. The same object can be viewed through zero counting, Im log zeta, random-matrix behavior, carrier-wave structure, or primes, and the span says that some apparent surprises dissolve only after that change of viewpoint.

So the trainable content here is perspective selection rather than a theorem. The introduction explicitly contrasts the dual readings of S(t) and says that unitary-matrix randomness is useful at some scales while prime information has to return at others. The program is to replace raw extrapolation from computations with controlled viewpoint changes.

units.title: Scalar modular bootstrap and zeros of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This span rewrites the scalar crossing equation at high temperature and shows that the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to the T^(c/2-3/4) envelope of the oscillatory subsubleading corrections.
units.interpretation:
In the paper's crossing-equation rewrite, the nontrivial zeta zeros appear as an oscillatory high-temperature correction whose envelope is T^(c/2 - 1 + Re(z_k)/2). RH is translated into a statement about that envelope rather than into a direct statement about where the zeros sit.

If every zero has real part 1/2, the whole oscillatory sector scales like T^(c/2 - 3/4); a zero farther right would enlarge that subsubleading term. The representation gain is precise: a zero-distribution claim becomes a bound on the size of a CFT asymptotic correction.

It states improved asymptotic, classical, and intermediate regions and lists the distinct ingredients behind the improvements: larger trigonometric polynomials, parameter optimization, sharper growth bounds in the critical strip, and a higher verified RH height.

units.title: A new integral representation for the Riemann Zeta function
units.selection_reason: The selected unit derives the paper's new integral representation for zeta by converting the alternating series into a residue-calculable integral and then summing inside the integral sign.
units.interpretation:
The derivation starts from the alternating series for zeta(1/2+ib) and identifies the obstruction directly: the summation over n cannot be carried out in its present form. The authors then choose an auxiliary integral with denominator x^4+n^2 so that a residue calculation reproduces n^(-ib)/sqrt(n) up to explicit factors.

That kernel choice is the mechanism. Once the series term is recoded as a residue, the sum over n can be interchanged with the integral and evaluated by a known summation formula, yielding new integral representations for zeta(s) in the strip 0<Re(s)<2, away from the simple pole at s=1.

units.title: Notes on the Riemann zeta Function-III
units.selection_reason: The theorem isolates the paper's main mechanism: a good Dirichlet series built from shifted zeta factors must have infinitely many poles in every right half-plane, with remarks extending the setup to derivatives and other L-functions.

units.interpretation:
The theorem isolates a pole-forcing mechanism. Start with a finite Dirichlet polynomial multiplied by shifted zeta-factors in the numerator and denominator; if that assembled object is still a good Dirichlet series, the source says it cannot remain meromorphic with only a sparse singular set.

Instead, poles must keep appearing in every right half-plane, even with one found in each interval [Y, Y + a log Y] for large Y. The remarks show that the same instability survives bounded derivatives and several L-function replacements, so the trainable object is the rigidity of the representation rather than one special zeta formula.

units.title: Elementary methods in the theory of L-functions, V. The theorems of Landau and Page
units.selection_reason: Despite OCR damage, this opening states the Landau/Page zero-repulsion and one-real-zero theorems and explains the stronger interval obtainable from Burgess's inequality.
units.context_limit: OCR damage obscures some displayed constants and intervals, but the theorem statements and comparison of proof strategies remain readable.
units.interpretation:
The opening states two linked zero-control theorems near s = 1. Landau's result says that two distinct real primitive character L-functions cannot both have real zeros too close to 1, while Page's theorem says that a single real non-principal character L-function has at most one simple real zero in the dangerous interval near 1. The span also notes that Burgess's inequality sharpens that interval.

The conceptual move is a zero-repulsion principle: exceptional real zeros are constrained collectively rather than behaving as independent accidents. The author also emphasizes a method change, replacing functional-equation or complex-function arguments with a simpler real-analysis route, while the exact constants are partially obscured by OCR.

units.title: Some consequences of the Riemann hypothesis
units.selection_reason: The note's opening states the exceptional-set improvement to the RH prime number theorem remainder and ties it to mean-square bounds and prime density in short intervals.
units.interpretation:
Assuming RH, the note claims an exceptional-set refinement of the prime number theorem remainder: outside a set of finite logarithmic measure, the error term improves from O(x^(1/2)log^2 x) to O(x^(1/2)(log log x)^2). The same span also gives short proofs of mean-square bounds for psi(x)-x and uses them to derive almost-all remainder estimates and a conditional normal-density statement for primes in short intervals.

The concrete move is to trade a uniform pointwise estimate for an exceptional-set formulation supported by average control. The finite logarithmic measure of the bad set is the key gain in this excerpt. Because the unit is OCR text, the interpretation stays at the prose level of the stated bounds and their relation rather than leaning on every damaged symbolic detail.

units.title: The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3·10^12
units.selection_reason: The source distinguishes claimed calculations from reproducible rigorous verification, then combines sign changes, Turing completeness, and interval arithmetic.
units.interpretation:
The span distinguishes local witnesses from global certification. Counting sign changes of the completed zeta function on the critical line only produces on-line zeros one by one; by itself that does not exclude missed or off-line zeros.

The extra move is Turing-style completeness. Once the local sign-change detections are paired with a rigorous global zero count, the computation upgrades from numerical evidence to a theorem that every expected zero in the verified height range has been accounted for. The switch from interval arithmetic to Arb and the decision not to over-isolate each zero are implementation choices in service of that certificate.

units.title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude

Riemann first uses an argument-principle count to estimate how many roots of xi lie in a bounded region, then reports that one indeed finds about that many real roots and says it is very probable that all roots are real. He immediately marks that stronger claim as unproved and unnecessary for his next step.

The operative move is disciplined separation of evidence and dependence. The source continues with a logarithmic product expansion over all roots alpha because that representation only needs control of root density and existence, not a proof that every root is real or an ordering of them on the line.

units.title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude
units.selection_reason: The Euler product is converted into a weighted prime-counting object and inverted through Mellin/Fourier machinery, exposing the bridge from primes to analytic singularities.
units.interpretation:
Riemann defines a symmetrized prime-counting function F and then folds prime powers into a weighted function f(x)=F(x)+1/2F(x^(1/2))+1/3F(x^(1/3))+.... With that choice, log zeta(s)/s becomes the Mellin transform of f for Re(s)>1.

The second step is inversion. By invoking Fourier's theorem in the Mellin setting, the paper writes f(y) back as a vertical-line integral of log zeta(s)/s times y^s. The unit is therefore a two-way transform bridge between weighted prime-counting data and analytic information in zeta, and it explicitly notes that naive termwise substitution does not yet converge, motivating the later integration-by-parts repair.

units.title: The De Bruijn-Newman constant is non-negative
units.selection_reason: Backward heat flow embeds RH into a monotone family with threshold Lambda, separating RH's upper bound from Newman's complementary 'barely true' lower bound.
units.interpretation:
The source embeds the RH question into the one-parameter family H_t evolving under backward heat flow. Newman provides the threshold constant Lambda such that H_t has only real zeros exactly for t >= Lambda, so RH becomes the upper bound Lambda <= 0. The paper's result is the complementary lower bound Lambda >= 0, obtained by contradiction.

The conceptual gain is that zero location becomes a dynamical boundary problem. Assuming Lambda < 0 forces increasingly rigid local-equilibrium behavior for zeros of H_0, and the source says that this rigidity conflicts with known local zero statistics for zeta, such as Montgomery-type pair-correlation information.

units.title: The De Bruijn-Newman constant is non-negative

units.context_limit: The v0 span ended before the final local-equilibrium contradiction.
units.interpretation:
The overview starts from the counterfactual hypothesis Lambda<0 and says the paper no longer pursues only improved Lehmer-pair bounds. Instead it strengthens the repulsion picture to a local-relaxation-to-equilibrium picture: if Lambda were negative, the zeros of H_t would tend to arrange themselves locally like an approximate arithmetic progression with gaps close to the average spacing predicted by Riemann-von Mangoldt counts.

The proof strategy makes that claim quantitative by combining interval zero-counting formulas for H_t, the ODE evolution of zeros under backward heat flow, and Hamiltonian and energy functionals with monotonicity properties. After truncation and averaging, those controls force near-equilibrium behavior at t=0, and the source says that this prediction is then contradicted by known local zero statistics such as Montgomery pair correlation. The obstruction comes from the mismatch between forced equilibrium spacing and the actual local distribution.
